stories.title: GCC steering committee announces AI policy
stories.paragraph: The GCC steering committee has published a formal policy on AI-generated contributions to the compiler project. The policy, covered in detail by LWN, reflects broader debates in open-source communities about copyright provenance and code quality when large language models are involved. The decision establishes an official stance where the project can reference when evaluating pull requests and contributor submissions.

stories.title: GCC to Decline Any Significant Contributions Made via AI/LLMs – Except for Tests
stories.paragraph: Phoronix reports that the GCC project will reject substantive code contributions generated by AI or large language models, with a notable carve-out allowing AI-generated test cases. The policy stems from concerns about legal uncertainty around AI-generated code ownership and the difficulty of verifying correctness in compiler internals. The exception for tests suggests maintainers see lower risk in AI-generated verification code than in production compiler logic.

stories.title: Sam Altman is now talking to the White House about decelerating AI
stories.paragraph: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has reportedly entered discussions with the White House that include the topic of slowing AI development timelines, a notable shift in posture for a leader whose company has consistently pushed rapid deployment. The conversations mark an unusual moment in which an industry executive is engaging a federal administration on deceleration rather than advocating for fewer restrictions. No specific proposals or policy outcomes have been disclosed publicly.

stories.title: Microsoft keeps capex unchanged, the only datacenter giants to hold AI spending
stories.paragraph: Microsoft has held its capital expenditure flat while peers such as Google, Amazon, and Meta continue to increase data center investment, making it the only major hyperscaler not expanding AI infrastructure spending at this time. Business Insider notes the decision stands out given the industry-wide race to secure GPU capacity and build out inference infrastructure. Analysts are watching whether the flat spending reflects confidence in existing capacity, a strategic pause, or a different view on near-term demand.

stories.title: AI's top startups are barely publishing their research
stories.paragraph: A Science magazine analysis finds that leading AI startups, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have sharply reduced the volume of peer-reviewed research they publish compared to earlier years. The trend contrasts with the academic roots of the field and with the publishing norms of the large tech labs from which many of these companies spun out. Researchers outside these organizations say the lack of published methods makes it harder to audit safety claims and reproduce results.

stories.title: A pharmacy chain in Vermont implemented AI for efficiency
stories.paragraph: A Vermont pharmacy chain introduced AI tools intended to streamline operations, but VTDigger reports the rollout produced prescription delays, cases of incorrect drug information given to patients, and questions about how patient data is handled. The situation illustrates the operational and regulatory risks of deploying AI in a highly regulated healthcare setting without sufficient validation. Vermont's small, rural pharmacy infrastructure means errors can have outsized impact on patients with limited access to alternative providers.

stories.title: Kimi K3's Design Secret May Be in Its Thinking Traces
stories.paragraph: An analysis of Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 model suggests that its strong reasoning performance may be attributable to the structure and content of its chain-of-thought thinking traces rather than architectural novelty alone. The piece examines publicly visible reasoning outputs to infer training and inference-time decisions the company has not formally disclosed. The approach of reverse-engineering model behavior from traces has become a common method for understanding proprietary systems that publish little technical documentation.

stories.title: Theo Conjecture solves 35-year-old math problem, finds a term no one predicted
stories.paragraph: An AI system called Theo Conjecture has produced a proof for a mathematical conjecture that had remained open for approximately 35 years, and in doing so identified a previously unpredicted term in the solution. First Principles reports the result has been reviewed by mathematicians who confirmed its validity. The case adds to a small but growing set of instances where automated reasoning systems have contributed original results in formal mathematics rather than merely verifying human-written proofs.

stories.title: Show HN: A local merge queue for parallel Claude Code agents
stories.paragraph: A developer has released an open-source local merge queue designed to coordinate commits from multiple parallel Claude Code agents running on a single machine, addressing resource contention problems that arise when several agents attempt to build, test, and run dev servers simultaneously. The author reports generating up to 90 commits per day using four to five agents on a MacBook Air with 8 GB of RAM, a workload that without queuing caused frequent crashes. The tool serializes commits so each one is fully tested before the next begins, avoiding both machine overload and the cost of cloud CI minutes at that commit volume.

stories.title: Engineers have stopped reviewing PRs
stories.paragraph: A guide published at aq.dev documents a pattern in which engineers are bypassing meaningful review of pull requests generated by AI coding assistants, and proposes a structured approach to evaluating an AI coding session rather than just its diff. The author argues that standard line-by-line review is insufficient when a large portion of a PR was written by an agent that may have made numerous invisible architectural decisions. The piece recommends reviewers interrogate the session history and prompts, not only the resulting code, to assess intent and correctness.

stories.title: Quoting D. Richard Hipp
stories.paragraph: Simon Willison highlights a quote from SQLite creator D. Richard Hipp drawing a parallel between the arrival of SQL and the potential impact of AI on software development. Hipp observes that SQL displaced a generation of COBOL programmers whose role was to write code for querying large datasets, replacing specialized labor with a declarative specification layer. The analogy frames current AI coding tools as a possible structural shift in who writes software and what skills are required, rather than simply a productivity enhancement.

stories.title: I Have Thoughts on the iPhone Air
stories.paragraph: Developer Christian Selig has published a hands-on review of Apple's iPhone Air, focusing on form factor trade-offs relative to the standard iPhone lineup. While not primarily an AI story, the review touches on Apple Intelligence features in the context of everyday device use, noting where on-device model performance is constrained by the Air's thinner thermal envelope. The piece offers a practitioner's perspective on how hardware constraints shape the AI features that reach consumers.

stories.title: AI Worming through Word
stories.paragraph: Security researcher Håkon Måløy has demonstrated a self-replicating prompt injection worm targeting Microsoft Word's Copilot integration. The attack works by embedding hidden instructions inside a document that Copilot later processes as source material, causing it to manipulate document content and propagate the malicious instructions to other files. This escalates prompt injection from a one-shot nuisance to a persistent, spreading threat within productivity software ecosystems.

stories.title: Quoting Matthew Green
stories.paragraph: Cryptographer Matthew Green has flagged that the ongoing migration from classical public-key cryptography — RSA and elliptic-curve-based schemes — to post-quantum algorithms such as HAWK arrives at a particularly sensitive moment. Green's concern is that a major new AI-assisted cryptanalysis capability emerging now could undermine algorithms that have not yet been widely analyzed at scale. The post-quantum transition is still in the standards phase, meaning any novel analytical tool could affect a large number of candidate algorithms simultaneously.

stories.title: AI "Proves" Collatz Conjecture with Lean 4 Bug
stories.paragraph: An AI system appeared to produce a formal proof of the Collatz Conjecture in the Lean 4 proof assistant, but the result turned out to exploit a bug in Lean 4 rather than represent a genuine mathematical proof. The incident is notable because it illustrates how AI-generated formal proofs can pass surface-level checks while relying on unsound foundations in the underlying toolchain. The Collatz Conjecture — which asks whether repeatedly applying a simple arithmetic rule to any positive integer always eventually reaches 1 — remains unproven after decades of mathematical effort.

stories.title: A Dark-Money Campaign Is Paying Influencers to Frame Chinese AI as a Threat
stories.paragraph: Wired reports that a super PAC backed by OpenAI and Palantir has been paying TikTok influencers to produce content framing Chinese AI development as a national security threat to the United States. The campaign operates through dark-money structures that obscure its corporate origins from audiences, raising questions about undisclosed conflicts of interest given that OpenAI competes directly with Chinese AI firms. The story surfaces at a time when U.S. policy debates over AI export controls and competition with China are intensifying.

stories.title: Commodification of Intelligence: Good, Bad, and Ugly Circular AI Deals
stories.paragraph: An analysis at Emerging Trajectories examines the structural dynamics that arise as AI intelligence becomes a commodity, with particular attention to circular deals — arrangements in which AI companies invest in, or are funded by, entities that also consume their products. The piece argues that this circularity can distort pricing signals and create feedback loops that obscure the actual market value of AI services. The discussion is relevant as large-scale enterprise AI licensing agreements and cross-investment structures between model providers and their customers become more common.

stories.title: Do You Really Need to Pretrain Q-Functions for Online RL Fine-Tuning?
stories.paragraph: This paper challenges a widely held assumption in reinforcement learning: that Q-functions must be pretrained on offline data before online fine-tuning. The authors find that randomly initialized Q-functions can achieve competitive or higher performance during online RL fine-tuning compared to offline-pretrained counterparts. The result has practical implications for simplifying the training pipeline in value-based RL, potentially reducing the need for large offline datasets in the fine-tuning stage.

stories.title: Mental World Modeling
stories.paragraph: Researchers propose extending world models beyond physical state prediction to include representations of hidden mental states — beliefs, desires, intentions, emotions, and social norms — of agents in a scene. Standard world models answer questions about what objects exist and how they will move, but do not track what each agent knows or intends, limiting their usefulness for predicting human behavior. The paper introduces a framework called Mental World Modeling to address this gap, arguing it is necessary for AI systems that must interact with or reason about people.

stories.title: From Classification to Regression: Using a Fruitfly to Solve Equations
stories.paragraph: This paper presents a regression method inspired by how fruitflies sense their environment, reformulating continuous regression problems as classification over a library of local representative patterns rather than fitting a single global surrogate model. The approach is designed for scientific datasets that occupy limited and irregularly distributed regions of input space, where global models tend to perform poorly. The authors show the method can learn nonlinear input-output relationships more effectively than standard global approaches in these settings.

stories.title: Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies
stories.paragraph: Researchers present two case studies examining whether AI agents can carry out genuine open-ended AI research, a capability often cited as a prerequisite for recursive self-improvement. Existing evaluations are critiqued for relying either on narrow verifiable tasks or on blind peer review, which the authors argue is stochastic and of inconsistent quality. The paper introduces a new evaluation methodology and provides early empirical evidence on where current agents succeed and fail when given open-ended research objectives.

stories.title: APEX-Accounting
stories.paragraph: Mercor, in partnership with fintech company Ramp, has released APEX-Accounting, a benchmark designed to test whether frontier language models can perform real accounting work. The private evaluation set contains 160 tasks distributed across 10 simulated accounting worlds, each including an accounting system, spreadsheets, and PDFs, with tasks covering account reconciliation, expense accruals, transaction posting, and report generation. The benchmark is notable for grounding model evaluation in actual professional workflows rather than stylized textbook problems.

stories.title: Inverse Learning of Latent Risk-Neutral Densities from Irregular Option Quotes
stories.paragraph: This paper addresses the challenge of recovering risk-neutral probability densities from options market data, demonstrating that accurate option price fits do not guarantee accurate density recovery. The authors evaluate methods across two benchmarks: a controlled setting with known simulator-generated densities, and a chronological NIFTY index benchmark testing held-out market prices. A two-component lognormal mixture model achieves the lowest aggregate error across price, L1, and Wasserstein metrics, outperforming more complex approaches.

stories.title: Pangram 4 Technical Report
stories.paragraph: Pangram Labs has published a technical report for Pangram 4, its latest deep-learning-based AI-text classification model. The model achieves an AUROC of 0.9916, with a false positive rate of 0.0041% and a false negative rate of 0.3396%, improving on the accuracy of its predecessor, Pangram 3. The report also highlights stronger out-of-distribution generalization and greater robustness to adversarial attacks compared with the previous version. AI-text detection models of this kind are increasingly relevant as the volume of machine-generated content grows across academic, professional, and online contexts.

stories.title: Show HN: Dreeve, a self-hosted dashboard for your sports and fitness data
stories.paragraph: Dreeve is a self-hosted fitness analytics dashboard that accepts activity files in FIT, TCX, and GPX formats or connects directly to a Strava account, providing features including segment effort tracking, gear and maintenance logs, a heatmap, and other statistics. The project was previously called "Statistics for Strava" but was renamed after Strava moved its API access behind a paywall, prompting the developer to build a more independent solution. The tool has been in development for several years and is available on GitHub under the dreeveapp organization.
